prompt: In many countries, a high proportion of young people who are released from prison commit further offences within a short period. What are the reasons for this, and how could the situation be improved?
essay:
Debate about youth reoffending tends to organise itself around a single question — whether sentences should be tougher or more lenient — and this framing has survived decades of evidence that it is the wrong question. Reoffending rates vary far more with what happens in the weeks after release than with the length of what preceded it. The useful inquiry is therefore narrow and practical: what does a nineteen-year-old actually have on the first Monday after the gate closes behind them?

Very often the answer is nothing that would hold anyone. No fixed address, since a tenancy could not be maintained from inside. No job, because the record is disclosable and an employer with other applicants has no reason to take the risk. No qualification, because the course was interrupted and no equivalent existed in custody. What remains is the same neighbourhood and the same acquaintances, now the only people offering anything at all. Under those conditions reoffending is not a moral choice reasserting itself; it is the path of least resistance in a situation deliberately emptied of alternatives.

The interventions that follow are unremarkable and unpopular for that reason. Housing arranged before release rather than applied for after it. A training place or job held open, agreed while the person is still inside. One named worker who does not change, so that the relationship survives the transition. Limiting how long minor convictions must be declared, so that a mistake at sixteen does not foreclose employment at thirty.

The objection is that this looks like reward for offending, and it is a serious objection. But the alternative is not a harsher outcome for the offender; it is a further set of victims, and a public paying for another custodial term. Choosing between principle and results is uncomfortable. Choosing principle and getting neither is worse.
title: Why young offenders return to crime
